subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 13 periods = 520 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 8h 40min

periods.textbook_anchor: Here Comes the Rain! — Students write at least two clues they think signal rain is coming and two clues that suggest it will not rain (p. 87)

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites children to look out of the window (or step briefly into the open) and describe the sky right now — colour, cloud cover, wind, smell of air. Children share observations orally in pairs.

Children open Textbook p. 87 and respond to the writing prompt: they record at least two clues that make them think rain will come and at least two clues that make them think it will not. The teacher circulates and asks follow-up questions: 'Who told you that clue? Where did you first learn it?'

A few children share their clues with the class. The teacher lists them in two columns on the board — 'Rain coming' and 'Rain not coming' — drawing out clues that come from elders, animals, plants, or traditional knowledge alongside scientific observation.
Children write one sentence in their notebooks: 'The best rain clue I know is … because …'. The teacher closes by noting that careful sky-watching is a skill people have used for a very long time.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record observations of a natural phenomenon by identifying and writing specific sensory and contextual clues.
periods.section_context: Sky observation for rain prediction, elder-knowledge clues about rain, two-column rain-clue writing task.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask children whether grandparents or neighbours have shared rain-prediction sayings involving animals, insects, or the colour of the sky — draw these out alongside scientific observation clues to honour both ways of knowing.

periods.activity_title: Watching Rain Fall: A Sensory Inquiry
periods.textbook_anchor: Here Comes the Rain! — Students observe rain closely, asking questions about intensity, drop size, direction, and slant, and collect rainwater in a vessel to check whether it looks clean or dirty (p. 88)
materials: Any available vessel or cup for collecting rainwater (or a small tray)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the inquiry questions from Textbook p. 88 aloud with the class: heavy or light? big drops or small? fast or slow? straight or slanting? Children predict answers for a recent or remembered rainfall before any observation begins.

If rain is currently accessible (or a recent sample was collected), children examine the collected rainwater in a vessel and respond to each question from Textbook p. 88 in their notebooks — one question, one observation per line. If no live rain, they recall the most recent rain they witnessed and write their remembered observations.

Pairs compare their answers: Did everyone see the same thing? The teacher facilitates a whole-class share, recording on the board the range of observations — especially whether children noticed the water looked clean or dirty, and guesses for why the direction of rain changes.

Children write one closing observation in their notebooks: 'The most surprising thing I noticed about the rain was …'. The teacher reinforces that noticing carefully and asking questions is the heart of inquiry.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a structured sensory inquiry by asking specific questions about a natural phenomenon and recording what they observe.
periods.section_context: Rainfall intensity, drop size, drop speed, rain direction and slant, collected rainwater appearance (clean or dirty).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask groups to compare whether the water in the vessel looked different from water they drink — this opens discussion about the difference between rainwater as it falls and what happens to it before we use it.

periods.textbook_anchor: Here Comes the Rain! — Students draw a picture of the rain they observed (p. 88)

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites children to close their eyes briefly and picture the last rain they observed — the sky colour, where the drops hit, what the ground looked like. One or two children describe their mental image aloud.

Children open to Textbook p. 88 and create their rain drawing, capturing their own observed rain — the intensity, direction, drop size, what the scene around them looked like. They are encouraged to be accurate to what they actually saw rather than a generic rain picture.

Children hold up or place drawings on desks for a gallery walk. The teacher asks the class to notice: Are all the rains the same? Do some show slanting rain? Heavy sheets? Small drops? Children point out one thing they notice in a classmate's drawing that is different from their own.

Children write the name of the rain they drew (e.g. light drizzle, heavy shower) and one sentence about what was happening in their picture. Teacher notes that each drawing is a personal scientific record.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present a personal observation of a natural phenomenon through drawing and a brief written label.
periods.section_context: Rain drawing showing intensity, direction, drop size, surrounding scene.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt children who draw generic rain to recall a specific rain moment — 'Was it the rain that came when you were on the way to school? What did the road look like?' — so the drawing stays grounded in real observation.

periods.textbook_anchor: What happened to the rainwater? — Students find out whether the rain fell only in their area or in other nearby places as well, make a guess first, then ask and find out (p. 89)
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram showing rainwater travelling into soil, puddles, streams, rivers, and underground

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'When rain falls, where does the water go after it hits the ground?' Children share ideas freely — puddles, soil, drain, river, underground. The teacher draws a simple sketch on the board showing rain falling onto different surfaces.

Children open Textbook p. 89 and discuss in small groups: Did the rain they observed fall only in their area, or did it fall in nearby places too? They make a quick guess first, then recall what adults or news told them about recent rainfall spread.

Whole-class share: groups report their guesses and what they found out. The teacher builds on the board sketch — adding absorption into soil, flow into streams and rivers, collection in ponds and lakes, and water soaking deep to feed wells — using children's descriptions to label each pathway.

Each child writes two sentences: where they think most of the rainwater in their area goes, and the name of any nearby stream, pond, river, or lake they know. The teacher closes by wondering aloud: 'Does all that water stay there forever?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can trace the observable pathways of a natural resource through the local environment by connecting personal knowledge with shared information.
periods.section_context: Rainwater absorption into soil, flow into streams and rivers, collection in puddles, ponds and lakes, groundwater feeding wells, spread of rain across nearby areas.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether any child has seen a dried-up pond or well come back to life after rain — this connects the abstract pathway of rainwater to a vivid, local, lived experience.

periods.activity_title: Songs and Feelings: Rain in Our Lives
periods.textbook_anchor: What happened to the rainwater? — Students find songs about rain or make one up in their own language and sing some songs about rain (p. 89)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a simple question: 'Does rain make everyone happy?' Children respond freely — some share that rain is welcome, others that floods or mud are difficult. The teacher acknowledges both without closing the conversation.

Children think of a song, rhyme, or chant about rain they know from home or their community — in any language. Working individually or in pairs, those who know a song write its first line; those who do not know one invent a two-line rain chant of their own and write it down.

Volunteers share or sing their lines. The teacher notes the range of emotions across songs — joy, longing, relief, fear — and asks: 'Why might some people feel differently about rain?' This naturally surfaces farmers waiting for rain, families worried about flooding, and children who love playing in puddles.
Each child writes one sentence: 'Rain makes me feel … because …' The teacher closes by noting that rain has always inspired songs and stories because water is so important to life.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express observations and feelings about a natural phenomenon through creative oral and written modes.
periods.section_context: Rain songs and chants in local languages, mixed feelings about rain, farmer dependence on rain, rain and flooding.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If children know a traditional seasonal rain song or a folk verse from their region, invite them to teach it to the class — this is a natural moment to honour the long relationship between communities and monsoon.

periods.activity_title: Our Local Water Body: Finding Out Its Name and Story
periods.textbook_anchor: What happened to the rainwater? — Students find out the name and some information about a stream, river, pond or lake near their village or city (p. 90)
periods.visual_aids: Board sketch of a local water body with labels for trees, birds, and surrounding land

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks the class to name every water body they know near their home, school, or village. Children call out names; the teacher lists them on the board. The class notices how many different kinds there are — pond, river, stream, lake, borewell, canal.

Children open to Textbook p. 90 and work individually to write what they know about one water body: its name, what it looks like, whether it is used for drinking, and what trees, birds, or animals they have seen around it. Those who have visited draw a quick sketch.

Children share in pairs, then a few share with the class. The teacher adds observations to the board sketch — naming the kinds of living things found near water bodies and asking why water bodies attract so many birds and animals.

Each child writes the name and one fact about their chosen water body in their notebook as a permanent record. The teacher closes by noting that these water bodies hold the rainwater the class traced in an earlier unit.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and record observable features of a local natural resource, including its name, use, and associated living things.
periods.section_context: Named local stream, river, pond, or lake; trees, birds, and animals near the water body; use of the water body for drinking.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether any child knows a poem or story about the river or pond they named — Textbook p. 90 also asks children to find a poem about a river, so this is a good moment to hear one if a child knows it.

periods.activity_title: Tracing Tap Water: Where Does Our Water Come From?
periods.textbook_anchor: Water is a Precious Gift! — Students discuss where they get water from and ask elders at home where the water that comes from the tap originates (p. 91)
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram showing the chain: tap → pipe → rooftop tank → supply pipe → well / borewell / tanker / river

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up a glass of water and asks: 'Before this water reached us, where was it?' Children respond freely. The teacher draws a simple chain on the board starting with the glass and working backwards — tap, pipe, tank, source.

Children open Textbook p. 91 and discuss in small groups: Does their home get water from a tap? A well? A tanker? Does someone carry water from a distance? They write their answers and draw a quick chain showing how water reaches them.

Groups share. The teacher completes the board diagram to show multiple possible sources — well, borewell, tanker, river, municipal supply — and asks: 'What happens when the supply is cut off? Do you store water? How?' The discussion naturally includes tanker delivery and irregular supply.
Each child writes: 'In my home, water comes from … and it travels through …' The teacher closes with the question from Textbook p. 91: 'Who carries this water? Say a big thank you to those people!'

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify the stages of a human-made water supply system by tracing the path water travels from its source to their home.
periods.section_context: Tap, pipe, rooftop tank, municipal supply, well, borewell, water tanker, someone carrying water from a distance.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether any child lives in a place where water does not come from a pipe — drawing out experiences of carrying water, waiting for tankers, or walking to a common well surfaces the reality of unequal access and prepares the class for the conservation discussion ahead.

periods.activity_title: Water Storage Vessels: Old and New
periods.textbook_anchor: Water is a Precious Gift! — Students ask grandparents or any elder how they got water, how they stored it, and what vessels they used, then write a short story about what they found out (p. 93)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of traditional water storage vessels (clay pot, clay surahi, copper vessel, brass pot, steel pot, aluminium pot, glass bottle, plastic bottle, plastic bucket) if available

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'What vessels does your family use to store water at home?' Children name them quickly — bucket, pot, bottle, tank. The teacher lists them on the board and asks: 'Did people always use these? What did they use before plastic and pipes existed?'

Children open to Textbook p. 93. Using the elder-interview prompt on that page as their guide, they write down what they recall from conversations with grandparents or elders about water vessels from the past — names, materials, special features. Those without elder knowledge draw or describe a vessel they have seen in a photograph, at a neighbour's home, or in their textbook illustration.

Pairs share what they found. The teacher builds a board comparison: past vessels (clay pot, surahi, copper, brass) alongside present vessels (plastic bucket, steel pot, glass bottle). The class discusses: Why did people use clay or copper? Are there any advantages that old vessels had? This surfaces the IKS thread about material properties and traditional craft knowledge.

Each child writes two sentences for their short story: 'My elder told me that in the past, people stored water in … They used it because …' The teacher notes that these vessels were made with careful knowledge about keeping water cool and safe.

periods.implied_lo: Students can compare past and present practices for storing a natural resource by drawing on elder knowledge and identifying the materials and purposes involved.
periods.section_context: Clay pot, clay surahi, copper vessel, brass pot, steel pot, aluminium pot, glass bottle, plastic bottle, plastic bucket; elder knowledge about past water storage; changes in storage practice over time.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether any child has at home a clay pot or surahi that is still in use — and why families might still prefer it over a plastic bottle for keeping water cool; this draws out traditional knowledge about material properties without labelling it separately.

periods.activity_title: How Much Water Do We Use? Listing and Estimating
periods.textbook_anchor: Water in Our Daily Lives — Students list all the activities they can think of for which we need water, and estimate how many mugs of water are needed to brush teeth and how much water is used to take a shower (p. 92)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks the class to name every single activity from the time they wake up that needs water. Children call out freely — brushing teeth, washing face, making tea, watering plants, flushing, cooking — while the teacher lists everything on the board without editing.

Children open Textbook p. 92 and complete the two writing tasks: first, their own complete list of water-using activities; second, their estimate of how many mugs of water they need to brush their teeth and how much water they use to shower or bathe. They write their estimates as a number and then mark whether they are confident or guessing.

The class compares estimates: the teacher asks two or three children to share their brush-teeth mug count and their shower estimate, then asks: 'Are we surprised by how much water these small tasks take?' The teacher writes the range on the board and the class discusses what would happen if the tap gave only one bucket of water per day.

Each child circles the ONE activity on their list that uses the most water. The class shares choices and the teacher notes that knowing how much water daily tasks need is the first step toward using it wisely.

periods.implied_lo: Students can estimate and record the water requirement of everyday activities, developing awareness of the quantity of water used in daily life.
periods.section_context: Water-using daily activities list, mug-count estimate for brushing teeth, water estimate for showering or bathing.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If a mug is available, hold it up and ask the class physically to guess how many of that mug would fill a bucket — the concrete reference helps children move from vague estimates to a grounded sense of water quantity.

periods.activity_title: Water Vessels Exhibition: Drawing and Sharing
periods.textbook_anchor: Water in Our Daily Lives — Students identify different vessels used to keep water at home, ask elders what vessels they stored water in, draw a picture of an interesting vessel, and put up an exhibition of these pictures in the classroom (p. 94)
materials: Tape or stick to display pictures on board or wall

time_bands.activity: The teacher reminds the class of the vessels named in discussion of traditional water storage. Today each child will draw one vessel they find interesting — from home, from elder knowledge, or one they imagined from a description — and add it to a classroom display.

Children open Textbook p. 94 for the vessel exhibition prompt. Each child draws one vessel on their sheet, writes its name in their own language, and adds any pattern or decoration they know it to have. They also write one line: why they chose it.

Pictures are put up on the board or wall. The class does a gallery walk, moving around to look at all the drawings. The teacher guides attention: 'How many different materials can you spot? Are there patterns on any vessels? Do any vessels look similar to each other?'

The class counts the different kinds of vessels drawn. Each child writes in their notebook: 'The vessel I found most interesting in the exhibition was … because …' The teacher closes by noting the range of craftsmanship and knowledge stored in these everyday objects.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present knowledge about a cultural object by drawing, labelling, and sharing it in a classroom exhibition.
periods.section_context: Water storage vessels drawn and named by children; vessel materials; patterns and decoration on vessels; variety of vessel types in the exhibition.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: As children do the gallery walk, ask them whether the vessels shown remind them of anything they have seen at a grandparent's house, a market, or a temple — connecting craft tradition to lived memory.

periods.activity_title: Building a Birdbath: Water for Birds
periods.textbook_anchor: Every Drop Counts — Students prepare a birdbath using a shallow container, keep stones in it for birds to perch, add fresh water, and maintain it by changing the water frequently and cleaning it twice a week (p. 97)
materials: Shallow wide container (old bowl, base of old pot, or similar — less than 10 cm deep)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a question: 'In hot summer months, where do birds get water to drink?' After brief discussion, the teacher introduces the birdbath activity from Textbook p. 97 — the class will build one together to offer water to birds.

Children follow the steps from Textbook p. 97: they select the container, place small stones inside for birds to perch, and add fresh water. If working as a class, one group assembles the birdbath while others observe and record the steps in their notebooks as a numbered procedure. If each group has materials, all groups build simultaneously.

The teacher leads discussion: Why must the water be changed frequently? Why must the birdbath be cleaned? What could happen if dirty water sits in it? This connects caring for the birdbath to the health of the birds and to the wider idea of stewardship.

Each child writes: 'I built this birdbath because … The birds that might come are …' The teacher notes that this is a small act of caring for another living thing and that people in many parts of India have always kept water outside their homes for travellers and animals.

periods.implied_lo: Students can build and maintain a simple structure that supports the water needs of birds, following a step-by-step procedure.
periods.section_context: Birdbath construction — shallow container, stones for perching, fresh water, frequency of water change, cleaning with scrubber.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask children whether they know of a tradition in their family or neighbourhood of keeping a pot of water outside the door for travellers or animals — this connects the birdbath activity to the wider cultural practice of sharing water that the section describes.

periods.activity_title: Water Pollution and Conservation: Thinking in Groups
periods.textbook_anchor: Every Drop Counts — Students discuss and list activities in their house or outside that pollute or waste water, think of three solutions to avoid wastage, and write them in their notebook (p. 99)

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses the situation: 'Imagine there is no water for a whole day. What could you not do? How would you feel?' Children share briefly. The teacher then flips the question: 'What do we do that wastes water without even noticing?'

Children open Textbook p. 99 and work in small groups on the Let us Reflect discussion task: they list activities at home or outside that pollute or waste water, then think of three concrete solutions to avoid wastage. Each group writes their list and solutions in their notebooks.

Groups share one waste-or-pollution example and one solution. The teacher records solutions on the board, grouping them: reducing use, reusing water, stopping pollution at source. The teacher asks: 'Which of these could you actually do starting tomorrow?' Each child marks one solution they will try.

Each child writes their personal commitment: 'One way I will save water is …' The teacher closes by noting that every small action adds up, and that keeping water clean and available for everyone — people, plants, animals — is a responsibility every person carries.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify sources of water waste and pollution in daily life and propose concrete conservation actions they can personally take.
periods.section_context: Water-wasting activities at home and outside, water pollution sources, three conservation solutions, personal water-saving commitment.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask groups whether they know of a community practice — a rule, a custom, or a shared norm — that protects a local water body from being polluted; this surfaces lived civic and cultural knowledge about collective stewardship.

periods.textbook_anchor: Every Drop Counts — Students write a few lines on their observations of the rain, write about a stream, river, well, pond or lake near their place, and draw their birdbath with the names of birds that visited (p. 98)
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram: the full water journey from rainfall → soil/streams/rivers/groundwater → household supply → storage → daily use → conservation

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws the full water journey on the board as a connected flow: rain falls → absorbed into soil, runs into streams and rivers, feeds wells and groundwater → water reaches homes through pipes, wells, and tankers → stored in vessels → used in daily life → must be conserved and protected. The class names each stage together, recalling what they know about rainfall, local water bodies, and household supply.

Children open Textbook p. 98 and choose ONE of the Let us Reflect writing or drawing tasks: either writing a few lines on their observations of rain, or writing about a stream, river, pond, or lake near their place, or drawing their birdbath and naming birds that might visit. Each child completes their chosen task independently.

A few children share what they wrote or drew. The teacher uses each sharing to point back to the water journey on the board — 'Your raindrop is right here at the beginning; your birdbath is a gift at the very end of that same journey.' The class discusses: Of everything in this chapter, what surprised them most? What will they do differently?

Each child writes one final sentence: 'Water is precious because …' Sentences are shared aloud to close the chapter. The teacher notes that water connects sky, earth, living things, communities, and traditions — and that taking care of it is something every person can begin right now.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect the stages of water's journey from rainfall to household use to conservation, expressing the whole as a coherent account in drawing or writing.
periods.section_context: Full water journey: rainfall observation, rainwater collection, local water bodies, household water supply chain, water storage vessels, daily water use, birdbath, water conservation and pollution.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: As children share their sentences, listen for whether they connect the natural and human-cultural threads — the rain that falls, the vessel that stores it, the tradition that shares it — and gently bring those threads together on the board if the class has not already done so.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya watched the sky before school. She saw dark grey clouds covering the whole sky and smelled the earth getting damp. What is the BEST conclusion Priya can draw from these clues?

options.label: A
options.text: It will be very sunny today.

options.label: B
options.text: It is likely to rain because she sees and smells signs that often come before rain.

options.label: C
options.text: It will be windy but not rainy because the clouds are grey, not black.

options.label: D
options.text: She cannot say anything about rain from looking at the sky.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. This item tests whether the student can use specific observed clues to support a prediction, as required by the sky-watching activity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record observations of a natural phenomenon by identifying and writing specific sensory and contextual clues.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not connected dark clouds and damp smell to rain — they may be naming a weather state without processing what the clues indicate.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has partial knowledge (grey clouds ≠ black clouds) but applies an incorrect distinction not supported by the section — a misconception about cloud colour as a threshold.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student does not believe sky observation yields useful predictions — this reflects a failure to engage with the core skill of reading natural clues developed in this section.

assessment_items.question_text: Rajan collected rainwater in a cup during a shower. He noticed the water looked slightly dirty. Write TWO questions Rajan should ask about the rain while he is collecting the water, AND give ONE reason why the collected rainwater might look dirty even though rain comes from clouds.
expected_elements: Any two valid inquiry questions about the rain's observable features — such as: Is it a heavy rain or a light one? Are the drops big or small? Is the rain falling straight down or at an angle? Do the drops come down fast or slow?

A plausible reason why collected rainwater might look dirty — such as: the rain picks up dust or particles from the air as it falls; the collecting vessel was dirty; the rain washed dust from surfaces into the vessel.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two of the inquiry questions modelled in the textbook activity. For the dirty-water reason, accept any response that identifies a plausible source of contamination — atmospheric dust, vessel cleanliness, or surface runoff — not just 'it is dirty because it rained'.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a structured sensory inquiry by asking specific questions about a natural phenomenon and recording what they observe.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Two specific inquiry questions about observable features of rain (intensity, drop size, speed, direction, or slant) — not questions about whether it will stop or about weather forecasts.
One reason connected to how rainwater picks up material from the air, a dirty vessel, or contact with a surface — not just a restatement that the water looks dirty.

assessment_items.task: Draw a picture of rain that you have personally seen. Show at least TWO things you noticed about it — for example, whether the drops were big or small, whether the rain was heavy or light, whether it fell straight or at an angle. Write one sentence under your drawing that names what kind of rain it was.
assessment_items.scaffold: 1. Think of a real rain you have seen. Close your eyes and picture it. 2. Draw the scene — the sky, where the drops fell, what was around you. 3. Add details showing two things you noticed. 4. Write one sentence below: 'This was a ___ rain because ___.'
format_of_output: A drawing showing rain with at least two observable features visible
One written sentence labelling the rain type and reason
assessment_items.annotation: Look for drawings that reflect a real observation rather than a generic rain picture — varied drop size, direction, intensity, or scene details are signs of engaged observation. The written sentence must name a specific feature, not just 'it was raining'.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present a personal observation of a natural phenomenon through drawing and a brief written label.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can translate a real sensory observation into a visual record and label it with specific observable features — showing that drawing is a mode of scientific recording, not decoration.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold walks the student through recall → drawing → annotation. A student who stops after the picture has completed part of the task; the sentence is what demonstrates the observational vocabulary.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: drawing shows at least two distinct observable features (e.g. slanting drops, heavy lines showing sheet rain) and the sentence uses a specific descriptor with a reason. Weak: generic rain lines with no differentiating features and a sentence that says only 'it was raining'.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle to draw may describe their rain scene in two or three written sentences instead; students with limited writing may label their drawing with single words (big drops, slanting, heavy) alongside a teacher-scribed sentence.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The textbook activity explicitly requires a rain drawing as a personal observational record; the sentence bridges the creative and scientific registers.

assessment_items.question_text: After a rainstorm, Kavya noticed that the puddle in her yard slowly disappeared over the next hour, even though it did not rain again. Where did most of that water MOST LIKELY go?

options.label: A
options.text: It evaporated immediately because of the sun's heat.

options.label: B
options.text: It soaked into the soil and joined the groundwater below.

options.label: C
options.text: It turned into clouds and went back up into the sky.

options.label: D
options.text: It flowed away into a river because all water moves to rivers.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. The section focuses on rainwater's journey into soil and groundwater at an observable, concrete level. Option A (evaporation) is plausible but is not the primary pathway introduced in this section for disappearing puddles.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace the observable pathways of a natural resource through the local environment by connecting personal knowledge with shared information.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student knows evaporation exists but applies it as the primary explanation for a disappearing puddle — mixing a concept not yet introduced in this section with an observation from it.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student conflates absorption into the ground with the return journey to clouds — a reversal of direction that suggests the water cycle concept is not yet secured at this stage.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student overgeneralises 'water flows to rivers', missing the absorption-into-soil pathway the section specifically develops.

assessment_items.task: Think of a rain that you remember. Write or sing two lines about how that rain made you feel. You may write in any language. Under your lines, write one sentence explaining why rain might make different people feel differently.
assessment_items.scaffold: 1. Remember a real rain — was it welcome? Scary? Fun? 2. Write two lines (a couplet, a chant, or just two sentences) about how YOU felt. 3. Think of someone whose feelings about rain might be different from yours — a farmer, a child in a flood-prone area, someone on a long journey. 4. Write: 'Rain might make ___ feel ___ because ___.'
format_of_output: Two written or dictated lines expressing a personal feeling about rain
One sentence explaining why rain affects different people differently
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any language. The two lines do not need to rhyme. The explanatory sentence must name a specific person or situation and a specific reason — not just 'everyone is different'. Regionally varied answers are acceptable and correct: a child in a drought-prone area and a child near a flood-prone river will have very different, equally valid responses.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express observations and feelings about a natural phenomenon through creative oral and written modes.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can use a creative written mode to express a real observation and then shift perspective to consider how the same phenomenon affects different people — bridging personal expression and social awareness.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Step 2 is the creative output; step 4 is the analytical step. A student who completes only the lines has done the creative part; the explanatory sentence is what demonstrates the broader connection the section builds.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: lines contain a specific sensory or emotional detail; the explanatory sentence names a real person type (farmer, flood-area resident) and gives a specific reason. Weak: lines are generic ('rain is wet'); sentence says only 'different people feel different things'.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may dictate their lines to the teacher or a peer if writing is difficult; students who prefer to draw their feeling may add a drawing alongside the sentence. Lines in any regional language or dialect are fully valid.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Short creative writing with a reasoning sentence
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The textbook task explicitly asks students to find or compose rain songs in their own language, making multilingual creative expression the intended mode for this section.

assessment_items.question_text: Meena lives near a small pond. Write TWO things she could observe about the pond to record information about it, AND write ONE reason why the pond is important for the living things around it.
expected_elements: Two observable features of the pond that can be recorded — such as: its name, what it looks like (size, colour of water, whether it is full or partly dry), whether it is used for drinking, the names of trees or plants around it, the birds or animals seen near it.

One reason why the pond is important for living things — such as: birds and animals come to drink from it; fish or other water creatures live in it; people use it for washing or drinking; plants near it get water from it.
assessment_items.annotation: Regionally varied answers are acceptable and correct — the specific name of the pond, the animals seen near it, and its uses will differ by location. Accept any observable feature and any plausible ecological or human use.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and record observable features of a local natural resource, including its name, use, and associated living things.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

expected_elements: Two specific, observable features of a water body — name, appearance, water level, surrounding trees or plants, birds or animals seen near it, or whether people use it for drinking or washing.
One clear reason why the pond supports living things — drinking water for animals, habitat for aquatic life, water source for plants, or use by people.

assessment_items.question_text: Water comes out of a tap in Arjun's home. Which of the following BEST shows the correct order in which water travels before it reaches Arjun's tap?

options.label: A
options.text: Tap → rooftop tank → pipe → river or well

options.label: B
options.text: River or well → pipe → rooftop tank → tap

options.label: C
options.text: Rooftop tank → river or well → pipe → tap

options.label: D
options.text: Pipe → tap → river or well → rooftop tank

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. The item tests whether the student can reproduce the direction of the water supply chain as traced in this section — from source to household, not the reverse.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify the stages of a human-made water supply system by tracing the path water travels from its source to their home.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has reversed the direction of the supply chain — they know the components but have not secured which end is source and which is destination.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student places the rooftop tank before the source, suggesting they see the tank as the origin rather than as a storage point along the chain.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student lists components in a random order, suggesting they recall the individual parts but have not understood the system as a directed pathway.

assessment_items.question_text: Dadi told her granddaughter that in the old days the family stored drinking water in a clay pot, not a plastic bucket. Write ONE way the clay pot was different from a plastic bucket for storing water, AND ONE reason why knowing about old storage vessels is useful today.
expected_elements: One specific difference between a clay pot and a plastic bucket for storing water — such as: a clay pot keeps water cool because clay is porous and allows slow evaporation; a clay pot does not add any taste or smell to the water; clay pots were made by local craftspeople using natural materials; plastic buckets are lighter and unbreakable.

One reason why knowing about old storage vessels is useful — such as: we learn about traditional knowledge and craft skills; some old vessels like copper or clay pots have properties (cooling, natural purification) that are still valuable; understanding change over time helps us appreciate what we have and what we have lost.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any plausible material-based difference; do not require the word 'porous'. For the second element, accept any reason that connects past knowledge to present value — whether practical, cultural, or historical. Regionally varied vessel names are acceptable and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare past and present practices for storing a natural resource by drawing on elder knowledge and identifying the materials and purposes involved.

competency.competency_text: Connects changes in the environment and the lives of their family and community, as communicated by elders and through local stories (changes in occupation, food habits, resources, celebrations, communication)

expected_elements: A concrete, material-based difference between clay and plastic as water storage materials — focused on how the material affects the water or the user (temperature, taste, weight, durability, origin).
A reason that shows the student values or can use elder knowledge about past practices — not just 'it is interesting' but a specific practical, cultural, or historical reason.

assessment_items.question_text: Neha is trying to find out how much water her family uses each morning. She counts that she uses 3 mugs to brush her teeth and 15 mugs to bathe. Her brother uses 2 mugs to brush and 12 mugs to bathe. How many mugs of water do Neha and her brother use together in the morning?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B (3+15+2+12 = 32). This item applies the mug-counting estimation skill from the section to a simple aggregation across two people — testing whether students can use their recorded estimates purposefully.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can estimate and record the water requirement of everyday activities, developing awareness of the quantity of water used in daily life.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student added only bathing mugs (15+12=27, not 30) or made an arithmetic error, not including the brushing mugs — showing partial aggregation.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student added only one person's total (3+15=18 or similar) — showing they did not aggregate across both people.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added correctly for one activity across both people (brushing: 3+2=5, bathing: 15+12=27, but summed only one pair) — a partial calculation error.

assessment_items.task: Draw ONE water storage vessel that you find interesting. Write its name in your language. Add one detail to your drawing — a pattern, a material, or a shape — that makes this vessel special. Below the drawing, write one sentence about what this vessel tells us about how people stored water.
assessment_items.scaffold: 1. Choose a vessel you know from home, from an elder's story, or from the classroom exhibition. 2. Draw it carefully — show its shape and at least one detail (pattern, colour, material). 3. Write its name in your language below the drawing. 4. Write: 'This vessel is interesting because ___.'
format_of_output: A drawing of one vessel with at least one visual detail
The vessel's name in the student's own language
One written sentence about what the vessel shows about water storage
assessment_items.annotation: Regionally varied answers are acceptable and correct — vessels named and drawn will differ by region and community. Accept any vessel that was discussed in the exhibition context. The sentence must say something specific about the vessel's material, use, or tradition — not just 'people stored water in it'.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present knowledge about a cultural object by drawing, labelling, and sharing it in a classroom exhibition.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can represent a culturally significant object through drawing and written labelling, showing that they engaged with the vessel not just as an image but as a carrier of knowledge about material, craft, and practice.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Steps 1–3 produce the drawing and label; step 4 produces the conceptual sentence. A drawing without the sentence shows observational skill but not the analytical step the section builds toward.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: drawing shows a specific vessel shape with at least one detail (pattern, lid, spout, texture); name is given in the student's own language; sentence mentions a specific property (keeps water cool, made of clay, has a pattern). Weak: generic round shape with no details; sentence is 'people stored water in this'.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot write the name may say it aloud and have it scribed; students who struggle to draw may describe the vessel in words instead. Any regional vessel is a valid choice.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Drawing with written label and sentence
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The textbook activity is specifically an exhibition of drawn vessels — drawing and labelling is the mode the chapter designs this learning for.

assessment_items.question_text: Rahul built a birdbath and placed it on his balcony in summer. After one week he noticed green slime growing on the stones and the water smelled bad. Write TWO things Rahul should do to fix this problem AND explain why one of those actions helps the birds.
expected_elements: Two correct maintenance actions — such as: clean the birdbath with a scrubber to remove the slime; change the water immediately and then change it more frequently; move the birdbath to a shadier spot to slow algae growth; rinse the stones.

An explanation connecting one action to bird welfare — such as: changing the water frequently means birds always have fresh, clean water to drink and do not get sick; cleaning with a scrubber removes slime that birds could slip on or that makes the water unsafe to drink.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two actions consistent with the birdbath maintenance procedure in the section. The explanation must make a clear connection between the action and the bird's safety or health — not just 'it helps the birds'.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can build and maintain a simple structure that supports the water needs of birds, following a step-by-step procedure.

competency.competency_text: Identifies needs of plants, birds, and animals, and how they can be supported (water, soil, food, care)

expected_elements: Two specific, actionable maintenance steps drawn from the birdbath procedure — cleaning with a scrubber, changing the water, rinsing stones, or adjusting placement.
A clear causal link from one action to bird welfare — the explanation should name the specific benefit (clean drinking water, no slipping, no illness) rather than a generic 'it is better for birds'.

assessment_items.question_text: Your school tap is left running while students wash their hands. Give TWO examples of activities in daily life that waste or pollute water, explain why each is a problem, and suggest ONE concrete action that students at your school could take to reduce water waste.
look_for: Two distinct examples of water waste or pollution drawn from daily life — at least one should be recognisable from a school or home context discussed in the chapter (e.g. tap left running, throwing waste into a pond or drain, using excess water for a task that needs little).

A clear explanation of why each example is a problem — not just 'it wastes water' but naming the consequence (less water available for others, polluted water cannot be used, animals lose a clean source).

One concrete, school-executable action — something students can actually do (turning off taps when not in use, reporting a leaking tap, placing a bucket under a dripping tap, making a sign reminding others to turn off taps) rather than a general statement.
A response that shows the student understands water is a shared resource — the strongest responses will connect individual action to community-level benefit.
assessment_items.annotation: Regionally varied answers are acceptable and correct — the specific sources of waste or pollution a child names will reflect their local context. Do not penalise a child who names a local water body or a locally relevant practice. Award full marks for two explained examples and one concrete action, even if the writing is brief.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify sources of water waste and pollution in daily life and propose concrete conservation actions they can personally take.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

look_for: Two specific, named examples of water waste or pollution — concrete enough that a teacher can picture the action (not just 'people waste water').
An explanation for each example that names a real consequence beyond 'it is bad' — water shortage for others, harm to animals, unusable polluted water.
One concrete, actionable conservation step that is clearly within a student's power to do in or around school.
The strongest responses show an awareness that water is shared — that one person's waste affects others — connecting individual behaviour to community resource.

assessment_items.question_text: Sunita traced the whole journey of water: it started as rain, soaked into the ground to feed a well, was pumped into pipes, stored in a clay pot at home, used for cooking, and the leftover water was used to water a plant. Explain how TWO stages of this journey show that water is precious, and describe ONE thing Sunita did that helped conserve water.
look_for: Two stages from the journey identified and explained in a way that shows why each stage makes water precious — for example: the stage where water soaks into the ground and feeds a well shows that groundwater takes a long time to collect and cannot be quickly replaced; the stage where leftover water is reused for a plant shows that once water has been used it can still serve a purpose rather than being wasted.
One specific conservation action identified from the journey — reusing cooking water for plants, storing water carefully in a vessel, or any other action Sunita took that reduced waste.

A response that connects the whole journey rather than treating each stage in isolation — the strongest responses will note that water that enters the ground as rain eventually becomes the well water that reaches the home.
assessment_items.annotation: This synthesis item draws on the full chapter. Accept any two stages the student can explain with a reason for why that stage reveals water's value. The conservation action must be one that actually appeared in the journey described — do not require a specific pair of stages.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect the stages of water's journey from rainfall to household use to conservation, expressing the whole as a coherent account in drawing or writing.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

look_for: Two stages from the full water journey (rain → ground → well → pipe → vessel → use → reuse) identified and explained — the explanation must go beyond naming the stage to say WHY that stage shows water is precious.
One concrete conservation action from the journey, described precisely enough that the teacher can see the student understands what was done and why it mattered.

The strongest responses show that the student understands the journey as a connected system — that rain replenishes wells, that stored water can run out, and that reuse extends a finite resource — rather than treating each stage as an isolated fact.
